 SNAP Participation Has Dropped. The Need Hasn’t.
 The Trump administration has called recent drops in nationwide federal food assistance enrollment good news. Food access advocates and hungry recipients disagree.
 By Rebekah Alvey 
 October 22, 2026
 Staff and clients at Telamon Corporation in Martinsburg, West Virginia, discuss changes to SNAP benefits under the Trump administration. (Phot credit: Rebekah Alvey)

 --> Within the halls of Congress and federal agencies, federal food assistance has become a major talking point. The Trump administration and Republicans on Capitol Hill have framed policy shifts to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program ( SNAP ) as cracking down on waste, fraud, and abuse in the program.

 But in the eastern panhandle of West Virginia, less than 100 miles away from the U.S. Capitol, those relying on SNAP and working with neighbors to navigate food insecurity paint a very different picture.
 Since Republicans in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill last July, 14,000 fewer West Virginians, including 4,000 children, are now on SNAP.
 “That number doesn’t share the need,” said Aly Nazarok, a housing counselor in Martinsburg, West Virginia. “That number shares the amount of people who now are unable to access that resource. And that is what we see boots on the ground every day, and that’s the sad and the scary part.”
 Nazarok works at Telamon , a national group that counsels low-income individuals on housing and budgeting.
 On a recent Wednesday morning, three clients and several case managers sat around tables with Civil Eats and explained how barriers to SNAP and the rising cost of food have made it challenging for West Virginians to lift themselves out of poverty.
 One case manager, Chelsea Garcia, works with several mothers now and said her guidance comes from experience. She was once a young mother relying on SNAP benefits and recalled the feeling of learning she’d lost access to benefits.
 “I thought I was gonna lose my flippin’ mind,” Garcia recalled thinking. “I don’t know what I’m going to do.”
 Two years ago, Jerome Lacks, a client and SNAP recipient, said he could fill his grocery cart with $100. Now, he’s left wondering where all the food is after spending the same amount.
 “You don’t get the same bang for the buck that you get nowadays,” said Jeffery Luff, a veteran, client, and member of the board at Telamon. The rising cost of food and housing, alongside stagnant wages in the region make it challenging to get by, he said.
 “You don’t get the same bang for the buck that you get nowadays.”
 On the national level, SNAP participation dropped by over 5 million people between July 2025 and June 2026, according to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. The latest numbers reflect a 17-year low for the program, despite no indicators the economy has significantly improved, according to the analysis.
 This drop is partially tied to direct policy changes, like stricter work requirements . But state administrators have also increased the amount of paperwork and verification for SNAP applications and reapplications, which means longer timelines and more hoops for families.
 Case managers at Telamon said they’ve noticed it’s more challenging to help their clients budget, given rising costs to housing, insurance, and food. Typically, Nazarok would advise clients to find places to cut back spending at the grocery store. Now, more and more clients are having to supplement grocery visits with food banks.
 Those resources are strapped, however, and facing an “onslaught” of additional need, said Yannick Mundy, a housing family mentor at Telamon. Food pantries in the area are simply running out of food or are left with limited commodities.
 Nazarok said pantries still haven’t recovered from the government shutdown in November 2025. It was the longest full government shutdown in history and the first time SNAP benefits did not go out as expected. Pantries and emergency food programs were expected to temporarily ease the need left by delayed SNAP benefits, but it put a major strain on local groups.
 One pantry located nearby in Jefferson County recently posted that it was in critical need and lacked basic items like pasta, Nazarok said.
 “That is like 99 cents, like, oh my goodness, what is happening?” Nazarok said.
 West Virginia food pantries are not alone. A recent NBC News survey of 90 major food banks found that 75 percent were seeing more demand. Simultaneously, 80 percent of surveyed food banks said they were getting less food from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
 In other words, the cuts to West Virginia recipients of federal food support have not been about waste and fraud. Rather, more people are going hungry or struggling to access food.
 Hunger Over Healthy Food 
 West Virginia was one of the early adopters of SNAP food restrictions . USDA has approved waivers in nearly half the states, restricting purchases of candy, soda, and other foods using SNAP benefits.
 The waiver took effect in West Virginia at the start of 2026, but it has been paused by a federal judge.
 Generally, the clients and workers at Telamon opposed the restrictions on certain foods in West Virginia and other states.
 At first, Sequoyah Spears, a Marine veteran and client at Telamon, said he thought the soda restrictions were “too much.” But later, he said it contributed to his transition to a healthier diet. He recently became a vegetarian and with the help of Telamon advisers, he’s started meal prepping with healthier foods.
 A Marine veteran and client at Telamon, said he thought the soda restrictions were “too much.” But later, he said it contributed to his transition to a healthier diet.
 Now, meals include more kale and trying new vegetarian options like soy corn dogs, he said.
 “I like the healthy approach,” Spears said. “That means longevity for myself, because it has caused me to make changes that bettered me.”
 Already he’s seeing results. His blood pressure has gone down, he said, his skin is clearing up, and he’s no longer pre-diabetic.
 At the same time, Spears said education and counseling were a big part of this transition. Those working with clients at Telamon said many West Virginians don’t have those resources or time to stretch SNAP dollars through meal prepping.
 Even Nazarok, who works three jobs, and her fiancé with a full-time job, have to spend time budgeting and being intentional about what stores to shop at in order to get the best deals on food.
 “I’m in a spot of privilege, but still our grocery bill is something that causes tension in our household,” Nazarok said. “We’re strapped.”

 A Policy That Overlooks On-the-Ground Realities 
 Under the Trump administration’s Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda, state and federal officials have emphasized whole, healthy foods, arguing that programs like SNAP need to prioritize nutrition. In practice, West Virginians may encounter barriers to healthy foods that make it challenging to transform that rhetoric into practice.
 While those sitting around the table at Telamon spoke about picking and choosing what grocery store they shop at for the best deals and food quality, Mundy noted those options are not available to many West Virginians.
 “No one has the time,” Mundy said. Instead, most of his clients just shop at Walmart or Family Dollar, which he said is lower-quality food and may not have as many whole-food options. Many clients are also working multiple jobs and may not have time to meal prep or think more holistically about meals, he continued.
 “Sometimes it simply won’t work in reality,” Mundy said about meal prepping.
 But the quest to access healthy foods may become even more challenging. This year, USDA finalized a rule increasing the stocking requirements for retailers that accept SNAP benefits. The Trump administration and supporters of the rule argue it will require SNAP retailers to offer more healthy foods.
 The changes are expected to largely impact smaller retailers like bodegas and convenience stores who may struggle to stock and sell a wider variety of goods. Groups representing convenience stores and anti-hunger advocates have warned this rule as is could cause some small stores to lose their SNAP authorization, which could make it even more difficult for recipients to access food.
 Recently, Senator Jim Justice (R-West Virginia) and 11 other Republicans sent a letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins, asking USDA to delay the rule by six months.
 “If a delay is not granted, tens of thousands of small format SNAP retailers will be unable to meet the requirements . . . meaning they will immediately be at risk of losing their authorization,” the letter said. “When that happens, the very households SNAP was designed to serve will lose critical access to food at the stores they have come to rely on.”
 In West Virginia’s eastern panhandle, public transportation is infrequent and unreliable, those at Telamon said. Without a car, a person may have to walk an hour and a half to travel five miles to the nearest market offering federal food assistance. The journey to a grocery store can present many hiccups.
 “If a delay is not granted, tens of thousands of small format SNAP retailers will be unable to meet the requirements . . . meaning they will immediately be at risk of losing their authorization.”
 Even if someone does catch a bus, Mundy and Spears said drivers may ask riders to get off if they have too many bags or items.
 Spears, who said he has “bad knees,” now relies on a roommate for transportation to the grocery store.
 Others may opt for walking to the grocery store, which in parts of West Virginia can involve miles up and down steep hills.
 Not only is the lack of transportation and accessible grocery store options a barrier to regular food shopping. It also impacts people’s ability to apply for and access social services like SNAP in the first place.
 Some clients at Telamon may walk to the state Department of Health and Human Resources (DHHR) for an appointment to apply for SNAP or other programs, just to learn they are missing one piece of documentation. Or it may be too late in the day to apply.
 “Every single day that happens,” Nazarok said.
 She recounted an instance where one of her clients walked a mile and a half to DHHR after work and was told they did not have time to see her that day and she would need to come back another day.
 Telamon employees have also watched clients’ kids or dogs outside DHHR so the client can go inside to fill out paperwork for SNAP or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).
 ‘Trapped’ on the Cliff
 As a former Marine, Spears said he’s learned to “adapt and overcome” obstacles. Part of his goal with meal prepping and shifting to a healthier lifestyle, he said, is to be prepared in case he no longer has access to SNAP dollars.
 Photo 2: Local goods at the Paw Paw market stand in stark contrast to many options available to SNAP recipients. (Photo credit: Rebekah Alvey)
 “If you got the ability to improve your situation, that’s what it’s designed to do,” Spears said of SNAP. But he also admitted that not everyone has similar means.
 Around the table at Telamon, everyone said that accessing SNAP was more challenging under recent policy changes. But more than that, once a family is on SNAP, West Virginians are “trapped” and struggle to improve their economic situation without losing those federal benefits needed to get over a hump, said Chelsea Garcia, a case manager at Telamon.
 The Telamon workers and clients spoke about what Washington and SNAP experts have long called the “benefit cliff,” where SNAP recipients can lose access to benefits if their wages even modestly exceed the income limits. Everyone at Telamon advocated for more wiggle room so individuals can build more economic stability before losing access to all federal benefits.
 Nazarok said that one of her current clients recently turned down a promotion for that very reason. The client is a mom with three kids; a raise at work would put her over the threshold for SNAP, but it wouldn’t be enough to make up for those lost dollars.
 “We did the math because I wanted her to take it,” Nazarok said of the raise. “It actually would cost her more money to take the promotion.” In the end, the mother passed on the promotion.
 “You lose all of those supports . . . the minute that you try to get better, try to make a better life for everyone around you,” Mundy said in describing his client’s calculus. “So, it’s like, ‘I’m not gonna push that envelope. I’m gonna stay right where I’m at.’”
